subject: tourism
description: Grade 12 Tourism, FET CAPS. To be merged into tourism-skill-tree.json. Mirrors the Grade 10 structure exactly: tiers = CAPS terms (T1-T4), mastery = 60% of a 20-item pool (FET, no timer), all skills unlocked (no prerequisites), learner-chosen order. Tap-based input types only (choice, true-false, cloze, sort-buckets, sequence, argument-builder, source-comparison) — no free text. 27 atomic skills covering professional image, conditions & contract of employment, codes of conduct, world time zones, world icons, attraction success, tour & route planning, itineraries, budgets, health & safety, travel documentation, World Heritage Sites & UNESCO, foreign exchange (strong/weak rand, conversions, BSR/BBR, exchange-rate effects), forms of international payment, global events & unforeseen occurrences, foreign market share, the three pillars, responsible tourists & codes of conduct, role players, customer feedback & satisfaction, service & profitability, and marketing South Africa.

levels.title: Grade 12 — Tourism
levels.description: The CAPS exit year, organised across four terms. T1: a professional image, conditions and contract of employment, codes of conduct and world time zones. T2: world-famous icons, what makes an attraction succeed, tour and route planning, day-by-day itineraries, tour budgets, health & safety and travel documentation. T3: World Heritage Sites and UNESCO, foreign exchange (strong/weak rand, currency conversions, BSR vs BBR, exchange-rate effects), forms of international payment, global events & unforeseen occurrences, and foreign market share. T4: the three pillars and responsible tourists, codes of conduct for tourist behaviour, role players in sustainable tourism, customer feedback & satisfaction, service & profitability, and marketing South Africa. 27 atomic skills, all unlocked, learner-chosen order.

atomic_skills.title: Professional image in the tourism industry
atomic_skills.description: How the image of the company (name, logo, slogan, website, stationery, marketing material, product packaging, appearance of the business, environmental and customer-service policies) and the image of the staff (professional appearance, uniforms, dress code, personal hygiene, grooming, interaction with customers, communication skills) build a professional image.

error_signatures.description: Confuses the company image with the staff image
error_signatures.example: Lists a uniform under 'company image' instead of 'staff image'

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Ask WHO the factor belongs to: the BUSINESS (logo, slogan, website, stationery, policies) = company image; the PERSON serving you (uniform, grooming, hygiene, communication) = staff image. Both together create the professional image.

atomic_skills.title: Conditions of employment
atomic_skills.description: Basic conditions of employment in a chosen tourism field (airlines, hotels or national parks): working hours, leave, remuneration and deductions, overtime, the role of the Basic Conditions of Employment Act and the Department of Labour in protecting workers.

error_signatures.description: Thinks conditions of employment are decided only by the employer with no legal minimum
error_signatures.example: Says an employer can set any working hours they like

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Remember there is a legal floor: the Basic Conditions of Employment Act sets minimums (hours, leave, notice). An employer may offer more than the minimum but not less.

atomic_skills.title: Contract of employment
atomic_skills.description: The contract of employment as the written agreement describing basic conditions: working hours, uniform allowances, travel benefits, leave, core duties, fringe benefits, remuneration and deductions, termination of service, professional accountability and service ethics.

error_signatures.description: Confuses a fringe benefit with a deduction
error_signatures.example: Lists a travel benefit as a deduction from pay

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: A fringe benefit is something EXTRA the worker GETS (travel perks, uniform allowance); a deduction is money TAKEN OFF pay (tax, UIF, pension). Sort each item by whether it adds to or subtracts from the worker.

atomic_skills.title: Purpose & value of a code of conduct
atomic_skills.description: A code of conduct for staff: its purpose (spells out expected conduct in performing duties and guides staff facing ethical challenges) and its value (creates a co-operative, collaborative atmosphere and promotes integrity in the workplace).

error_signatures.description: Treats a staff code of conduct as the same thing as a job contract
error_signatures.example: Says a code of conduct lists a worker's salary

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: A code of conduct is about BEHAVIOUR and ethics (how staff should act); a contract is about TERMS (pay, hours, leave). The code guides decisions; the contract sets the deal.

atomic_skills.title: World time zones
atomic_skills.description: Time-zone concepts (UTC, Greenwich, hemispheres, equator, standard time, local time, the international date line, the 24-hour clock, latitude and longitude); reading a world time-zone map; daylight saving time; simple calculations of arrival and departure times; and jet lag, its symptoms and how to ease it.

error_signatures.description: Adds time when travelling west or subtracts when travelling east
error_signatures.example: Says flying from Johannesburg west to New York makes the local time later, not earlier

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Travel EAST = clocks go FORWARD (add hours); travel WEST = clocks go BACK (subtract hours). UTC is the world reference time at Greenwich; add a place's offset to find its local time.

atomic_skills.title: World-famous icons & attractions
atomic_skills.description: The difference between an attraction and an icon; why certain attractions or physical features are regarded as icons; the location (country and city/area) of world-famous icons such as the Eiffel Tower, Taj Mahal, Great Wall of China, Statue of Liberty, Sydney Opera House, Christ the Redeemer, Colosseum, Big Ben, the Pyramids of Giza and Machu Picchu; and the economic significance of icons for a country.

error_signatures.description: Places a world icon in the wrong country
error_signatures.example: Says the Taj Mahal is in Pakistan rather than India

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Learn each icon as a pair: icon → country (and city). An icon is more than an attraction — it is instantly recognised and stands as a symbol of its country, e.g. Eiffel Tower → Paris, France.

atomic_skills.title: Factors contributing to the success of a tourist attraction
atomic_skills.description: Factors behind a successful attraction (excellent marketing, sustainable and responsible management, efficient and ethical staff, positive visitor experience, safety and crime prevention, good appearance and upkeep, universal access for people with disabilities) and the characteristics of success (visitor numbers exceed targets, repeat visits, income exceeds target, positive impact on the local community and environment).

error_signatures.description: Confuses a factor that CAUSES success with a sign that an attraction IS successful
error_signatures.example: Lists 'repeat visits' as a factor that creates success rather than a characteristic of it

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Separate cause from result: FACTORS are things management does (market well, keep it safe and clean, train staff); CHARACTERISTICS are measurable results (visitor numbers and income beat targets, visitors return).

atomic_skills.title: Tour plans & route planning
atomic_skills.description: Developing a tour plan to suit a tourist's profile, budget and available time; route planning; and choosing transport, accommodation, attractions and activities that match the customers' needs and preferences.

error_signatures.description: Plans a tour that ignores the tourist's profile, budget or time
error_signatures.example: Books five-star lodges for a backpacker on a tight budget

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Start from the tourist PROFILE (who they are, how much money and time they have, what they like), then choose transport, accommodation and activities to fit it. The plan must suit the tourist, not the other way round.

atomic_skills.title: Compiling a day-by-day itinerary
atomic_skills.description: The main aspects of an itinerary (transport, accommodation, attractions, activities and stops for meals); factors to consider when drawing one up (logical planning, sensible spread, variety and appropriateness); and arranging the days of a trip in a logical order.

error_signatures.description: Plans days that backtrack or ignore logical geography
error_signatures.example: Drives a group from Cape Town to Durban and back to Cape Town between two nearby stops

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Plan in a logical line: group nearby places together, avoid backtracking, keep travel times sensible, and spread activities with variety and rest. An itinerary should flow smoothly day by day.

atomic_skills.title: Compiling a tour budget
atomic_skills.description: Factors influencing the development of a tour budget and drawing up a basic budget showing expenses for travel, accommodation, meals, entrance to attractions, shopping and tips; simple addition of costs and working out what fits within a given budget.

error_signatures.description: Leaves out cost items or miscounts the total
error_signatures.example: Forgets to include meals and tips when totalling a tour budget

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: List every cost type (travel, accommodation, meals, attractions, shopping, tips), add them up carefully, then compare the total with the money available. If it is over budget, cut or downgrade an item.

atomic_skills.title: Health & safety for travellers
atomic_skills.description: Health concepts (World Health Organisation, health certificates, travel clinics, compulsory and recommended vaccinations such as yellow fever); precautions for high-risk areas (malaria, bilharzia, cholera; bottled water, sun block, preventative medicine); and general safety precautions for tourists in a car, in public, in a hotel room, at the airport and after dark.

error_signatures.description: Confuses a health precaution with a safety precaution
error_signatures.example: Lists taking malaria tablets as a 'safety' measure rather than a 'health' measure

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: HEALTH precautions protect against illness (vaccinations, tablets, bottled water); SAFETY precautions protect against crime and accidents (lock doors, don't flash valuables, be careful after dark). Ask: illness or harm?

atomic_skills.title: Travel documentation
atomic_skills.description: Travel documents needed to visit a country (valid passport, visa, health certificate); obtaining a passport, visa and international driver's licence; and customs concepts — duty-free goods, prohibited goods, the green and red channels, to declare and travel allowances.

error_signatures.description: Confuses the green and red customs channels
error_signatures.example: Says a traveller with goods to declare should use the green channel

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: GREEN channel = nothing to declare; RED channel = goods to declare or over the allowance. A passport identifies you; a visa is permission to enter a specific country. Match each document and channel to its job.

tiers.title: Term 3 — World Heritage Sites, foreign exchange & international travel

atomic_skills.title: World Heritage Sites & the role of UNESCO
atomic_skills.description: The concept of a World Heritage Site; the role of UNESCO (its logo and main function of identifying and protecting sites of outstanding universal value); the difference between natural and cultural World Heritage Sites; and the value of World Heritage status to a country's tourism industry.

error_signatures.description: Confuses natural and cultural World Heritage Sites, or thinks the site owner declares the status
error_signatures.example: Calls a fossil hominid site a cultural site, or says a country awards itself World Heritage status

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: UNESCO (a United Nations body) declares and protects World Heritage Sites — not the site owner. NATURAL = made by nature (landscapes, fossils, wetlands); CULTURAL = made by people (buildings, rock art, settlements).

atomic_skills.title: World Heritage Sites in South Africa
atomic_skills.description: South Africa's World Heritage Sites and their type and location — the Cradle of Humankind, Robben Island, iSimangaliso (Greater St Lucia) Wetland Park, uKhahlamba-Drakensberg Park, Mapungubwe, the Cape Floral Region, the Vredefort Dome, the Richtersveld and the Barberton Makhonjwa Mountains — and how each meets UNESCO criteria.

error_signatures.description: Misclassifies a South African site or places it in the wrong province
error_signatures.example: Calls Robben Island a natural site, or places the Cradle of Humankind in the Western Cape

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: For each South African site, learn its type (natural or cultural) and province. Robben Island and Mapungubwe are cultural (human history); iSimangaliso and the Cape Floral Region are natural (ecosystems); the Cradle of Humankind (fossils) is in Gauteng.

atomic_skills.title: The strong & weak rand
atomic_skills.description: The concepts of a strong and a weak rand; the relative strength or weakness of a currency at a given time; the link to gross domestic product (GDP) and the multiplier effect; and how a strong or weak rand affects the buying power of South Africans abroad and the cost of South Africa for inbound tourists.

error_signatures.description: Thinks a strong rand is always good for tourism, or reverses who benefits
error_signatures.example: Says a weak rand makes South Africa expensive for foreign tourists

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: A STRONG rand buys more foreign currency — good for South Africans travelling out, but makes SA pricier for inbound tourists. A WEAK rand is the opposite: cheaper for inbound tourists, dearer for outbound South Africans. Ask who is travelling which way.

atomic_skills.title: Currency conversions
atomic_skills.description: Reading a currency rate sheet and converting between South African rand and major currencies using rates given as 1 unit of foreign currency = a value in rand (e.g. 1 USD = R18). Working out how much foreign currency a rand amount buys, and how many rand a foreign amount costs, rounded to two decimals.

error_signatures.description: Multiplies when they should divide (or vice versa) when converting
error_signatures.example: Divides rand by the rate to get foreign currency when they should follow the rate given

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Use the rate exactly as written in the question. If 1 USD = R18, then to find rand multiply dollars by 18; to find dollars divide rand by 18. Always check the answer makes sense in size.

atomic_skills.title: Bank selling rate vs bank buying rate
atomic_skills.description: The difference between the bank selling rate (BSR) and the bank buying rate (BBR); which rate applies when a traveller buys foreign currency before a trip and which applies when they sell unused foreign currency back; and why the two rates differ (the bank's margin).

error_signatures.description: Applies the BBR when the customer is buying foreign currency
error_signatures.example: Says you use the bank buying rate to buy dollars before a holiday

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Read the rate from the BANK's point of view. BSR (bank SELLING) = the bank sells you foreign currency (you buy before the trip). BBR (bank BUYING) = the bank buys back your leftover foreign currency. The selling rate is less favourable to you.

atomic_skills.title: Effect of exchange-rate fluctuations on tourism
atomic_skills.description: How rises and falls in the exchange rate affect both inbound and outbound tourism; how a weak or strong rand changes the travel patterns of South Africans heading to developing and developed countries; and the impact of fluctuations on the affordability of destinations.

error_signatures.description: Cannot trace a rate change through to its effect on tourist numbers
error_signatures.example: Says a weakening rand will reduce the number of foreign tourists coming to South Africa

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Trace the chain: a weaker rand makes SA CHEAPER for inbound tourists (more arrivals) and makes overseas trips DEARER for South Africans (fewer outbound). A stronger rand reverses both. Follow the money to the tourist's wallet.

atomic_skills.title: Forms of payment when travelling internationally
atomic_skills.description: Forms of payment for international travel — electronic fund transfers (EFT), telegraphic/SWIFT transfers, bank drafts, internet payments, foreign bank notes (cash), credit cards, traveller's cheques and preloaded foreign-currency cards — and the advantages and disadvantages of each.

error_signatures.description: Mismatches a payment form with its main advantage or disadvantage
error_signatures.example: Says carrying large amounts of cash is the safest form of payment abroad

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Weigh each form on safety, convenience and cost. Cash is convenient but risky if lost or stolen; cards and preloaded cards are safer and can be cancelled; traveller's cheques are replaceable but less widely accepted today.

atomic_skills.title: Global events & unforeseen occurrences
atomic_skills.description: The concept of a global event (e.g. the FIFA World Cup, Olympic Games); the positive and negative impact of hosting on international and domestic tourism and on the host economy (infrastructure, investment, foreign-exchange income, the multiplier effect); and unforeseen occurrences of international significance (natural disasters, disease, recession, political unrest, terrorism) and their impact on tourism.

error_signatures.description: Confuses a planned global event with an unforeseen occurrence
error_signatures.example: Lists an earthquake as a 'global event' that a country chooses to host

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: A GLOBAL EVENT is planned and hosted on purpose (World Cup, Olympics) and usually boosts tourism; an UNFORESEEN OCCURRENCE is sudden and unwanted (tsunami, pandemic, unrest) and usually harms it. Ask: planned or unexpected?

atomic_skills.title: Foreign market share & inbound statistics
atomic_skills.description: Interpreting inbound international tourism statistics — foreign arrivals to South Africa (land and air), how arrivals determine foreign market share, the most-visited provinces, length of stay, average expenditure per tourist and activities undertaken — using sources such as StatsSA and South African Tourism reports.

error_signatures.description: Misreads a statistics table or confuses market share with raw arrivals
error_signatures.example: Reads the column for length of stay as the number of arrivals

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Read the table heading and units before answering. Market SHARE is a country's portion of total arrivals (a percentage of the whole); raw arrivals is a count. Match each question to the correct column.

tiers.title: Term 4 — Responsible tourism, customer satisfaction & marketing SA

atomic_skills.title: The three pillars & responsible tourists
atomic_skills.description: The three pillars of sustainable tourism (people, profit, planet) and the triple bottom-line approach; good environmental practices (resource, waste and pollution management; indigenous flora; control of alien plants); the responsible role of business (ownership, employment, local procurement); social effects and corporate social investment (CSI); and what makes a responsible tourist.

error_signatures.description: Sorts an action under the wrong pillar
error_signatures.example: Places 'recycling waste' under People instead of Planet

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Match each action to its pillar: PLANET = the environment (energy, water, waste, wildlife); PEOPLE = communities and culture (jobs, CSI, respect); PROFIT = the business running responsibly and staying viable. Ask which the action mainly protects.

atomic_skills.title: Codes of conduct & demand for responsible tourism
atomic_skills.description: Codes of conduct for tourist behaviour (social, economic and environmental); how a destination can attract responsible, conscious tourists; the growing demand for responsible tourism; and the role of Fair Trade Tourism South Africa (FTTSA) in encouraging responsible and sustainable practices.

error_signatures.description: Cannot classify a behaviour as social, economic or environmental
error_signatures.example: Calls 'buying local crafts' an environmental rather than an economic action

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Sort responsible behaviour by the pillar it serves: SOCIAL = respect people and culture; ECONOMIC = support local business and fair pay; ENVIRONMENTAL = protect nature and reduce waste. FTTSA certifies businesses meeting these standards.

atomic_skills.title: Role players in responsible & sustainable tourism
atomic_skills.description: The role players who drive responsible and sustainable tourism — government and local authorities, tourism businesses, communities, tourists themselves and organisations such as FTTSA — and how each contributes through policy, practice, behaviour and certification.

error_signatures.description: Assigns a responsibility to the wrong role player
error_signatures.example: Says individual tourists set national tourism policy

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Match the job to the player: GOVERNMENT makes policy and laws; BUSINESSES run sustainably and create jobs; COMMUNITIES protect heritage and benefit locally; TOURISTS behave responsibly; FTTSA certifies fair-trade operators.

atomic_skills.title: Customer feedback & measuring satisfaction
atomic_skills.description: The concept and purpose of customer feedback; methods to obtain it (surveys, questionnaires, feedback cards, follow-up calls, SMS messages, web-based responses); and how to analyse feedback — capturing the data, identifying common complaints, deciding on an action plan and starting an intervention — to measure customer satisfaction.

error_signatures.description: Thinks gathering feedback alone improves service, with no analysis or action
error_signatures.example: Says handing out feedback cards is enough, without acting on the results

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Feedback is a cycle: COLLECT (surveys, cards, calls) → ANALYSE (find common complaints) → ACT (make an action plan) → IMPROVE (start the intervention). Collecting without acting changes nothing.

atomic_skills.title: Service differences & profitability
atomic_skills.description: Reasons why the level of service differs from one organisation to another (training, staff attitude, management, resources, standards) and the impact of the service an organisation delivers on its business profitability — how good service builds repeat business and reputation while poor service drives customers away.

error_signatures.description: Does not link service quality to profit
error_signatures.example: Says the standard of service has no effect on how much money a business makes

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Trace the link: good service → satisfied customers → repeat visits, recommendations and good reviews → more income and profit. Poor service → lost customers and bad reputation → falling profit. Service and profit are connected.

atomic_skills.title: Marketing South Africa as a tourism destination
atomic_skills.description: The importance of marketing South Africa internationally (more foreign arrivals, greater awareness); the core business of South African Tourism; marketing opportunities such as ITB Berlin, the World Travel Market, the Tourism Indaba and the Getaway show; the funding role of TOMSA; and the concept of branding and South Africa's brand logo.

error_signatures.description: Confuses the bodies and events that market South Africa
error_signatures.example: Says TOMSA is a trade show rather than the levy that funds marketing

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Keep the roles straight: SA TOURISM markets the country internationally; TOMSA is the levy that FUNDS that marketing; the INDABA, ITB Berlin and World Travel Market are trade SHOWS where SA is promoted. Match each name to its job.
